standards.name: Access to Biological Collection Data (ABCD) Schema
standards.abstract: ABCD is a comprehensive XML schema for sharing primary biodiversity data about specimens and observations (collection units). It models datasets containing units (specimens/observations), dataset-level metadata (contacts, descriptions, licenses), and detailed unit records including identifications, gathering events, locality coordinates, multimedia links and more. The standard is published and maintained by Biodiversity Information Standards (TDWG) and the ABCD Maintenance Group; it originated as an XML schema (development from 2001, ratified v2 in 2005) and is available in multiple versions (notably 2.06 and 3.0). ABCD's scope covers structured interchange of biological collection records across institutions and networks (e.g. GBIF, BioCASe), providing highly structured element definitions (XML Schema) and parallel support for atomised data and free-text representations.

classification.rationale: The source material is an XML Schema (XSD) with explicit element names and typed structure (e.g. DataSet, Unit, Gathering, specific subelements like UnitID, SourceInstitutionID, DateTime, FileURI). This is a genuine field-level specification (not prose checklist or ordered stages), so it best corresponds to a TABLE.

standards.notes: I extracted a representative subset of ABCD's explicit element-level fields from the XML Schema and sample documents (Dataset-level elements, Unit identifiers, gathering/location fields, multimedia link, taxon name). The ABCD standard is large; the source includes full XSD files (v2.06, 2.06f, 2.1, 3.0 and application subsets) that enumerate many additional elements and types. If you want, I can: (a) expand this table to include every element from a chosen XSD version (e.g. ABCD 2.06f or ABCD 3.0), (b) emit machine-readable JSON Schema/CSV mapping for a selected subset, or (c) extract controlled vocabularies and enumerated value lists referenced by ABCD.

standards.name: ABCD 3.0 Ontology (ABCD OWL)
standards.abstract: The ABCD 3.0 Ontology models biodiversity collection and observation data (specimens, units, multimedia objects, identifications, gatherings, etc.) as an OWL/RDF vocabulary. It describes classes (core concepts such as Specimen Unit, Multimedia Object), object properties (relations between classes), datatype properties (literal-valued attributes), individuals (members of controlled vocabularies) and metaproperties. The material is published by the TDWG ABCD Task Group / Biodiversity Information Standards (TDWG) and distributed as an OWL ontology (RDF/XML). The ontology addresses the problem of interoperable exchange and semantic description of biodiversity collection data and related metadata; scope covers 64 classes, 88 object properties, 301 datatype properties and 79 individuals (as stated in the source) and includes inheritance, subproperties, and mappings to external terminologies.

classification.rationale: The source is an OWL ontology that enumerates concrete named entities (Classes, Object Properties, Datatype Properties, Individuals, Metaproperties) each with metadata (labels, comments, status, dates). This presents genuine field-level structure (explicit named ontology elements and counts) rather than prose guidance or an ordered workflow, so it is best represented as a metadata table of ontology components.

Classes.name: Classes
Classes.descr: Ontology classes (core concepts) defined in the ABCD ontology.
Classes.evidence: There are 64 classes, which express the core concepts of ABCD. The most general class is “Data Set” but unlike in the XML Version, there is no implicit hierarchy of the classes.

Object_Properties.name: Object Properties
Object_Properties.descr: Object properties connecting classes (relations between ontology classes).
Object_Properties.evidence: There are 88 object properties in total, all of which have a specified range for the class they are connecting to. Only 4 however have a specified domain, which defines the class by which an object property can be used (“has Inverse Association” which links from an Association to an Association, “has Type Specific Information” which gives additional information for a Unit class as well as “has Permit Status” and “has Permit Type” which both link to controlled vocabularies only applicable to the Permit class). For all other object properties, the implicit domain is owl:Thing, allowing flexible reuse of the object properties.

Datatype_Properties.name: Datatype Properties
Datatype_Properties.descr: Datatype properties (literal-valued attributes; analogous to leaf elements in the XML schema).
Datatype_Properties.evidence: Datatype Properties are the counterpart of leaf-elements in the XML Schema. They are used to connect values of a specific type to classes. Some of the 301 Datatype Properties of the ontology are very generic so they can often be reused (e.g. notes) others are more closely related to a specific class (e.g. fullScientificName).

Individuals.name: Individuals
Individuals.descr: Named individuals used as members of controlled vocabularies within the ontology.
Individuals.evidence: The 79 Individuals of the ontology are each belonging to one of the 8 controlled vocabularies of the ontology. They are in fact instances of the vocabulary class and are used to express ABCD in RDF.

Metaproperties.name: Metaproperties
Metaproperties.descr: Properties that describe other properties (e.g. preferred, sequence).
Metaproperties.evidence: The Metaproperties preferred and sequence are Properties that can be used to describe other properties. When e.g. a Unit Class is connected to multiple Identification Classes by several hasIdentification Object-Poperties, the metaproperty is used to indicate which of the hasIdentification Properties is preferred over the others. A sequence can be used to order identical properties connected to the same class and can e.g. be used to describe the importance of Identifiers (hasIdentifier).

Ontology_Format.name: Ontology format / modelling
Ontology_Format.descr: Representation format and grouping used by the standard.
Ontology_Format.evidence: The ABCD 3.0 Ontology is modelled as an OWL Ontology. All concept in the ontology belong to one of four groups: Classes, Object Properties, Datatype Properties or Individuals.

standards.notes: This extraction preserves the main structural elements the source enumerates (classes, properties, individuals, metaproperties) and quotes key descriptive passages verbatim. The original OWL file contains many individual class and property definitions (examples such as Accession, Annotation, Assemblage, Association, AudioObject, BacterialScientificName, Biotope, etc.) which can be further enumerated into the table if a full element-level dump is required.

standards.name: Access to Biological Collection Data Extended for Geosciences (ABCDEFG)
standards.abstract: The EFG (Extension for Geosciences) extends the ABCD schema to represent earth-science collection items (fossils, rocks, minerals, sediments, boreholes, stratigraphic sections) and associated observations, analyses and dates. The extension is expressed as an XML Schema Definition (XSD) and a set of controlled terms, intended to enable detailed, interoperable metadata exchange for petrological, mineralogical and paleontological collection data. It is maintained by a TDWG Task Group and has been submitted for TDWG ratification; development began within the SYNTHESYS/GeoCASe projects.

classification.rationale: The provided source materials are descriptive prose about the EFG extension (abstract, background, task group charter, and public-review announcement) rather than a literal table of fields or a stepwise workflow. The materials describe scope, goals, maintenance and where the XSD is hosted, which are guidance/principles rather than a field-level metadata table or a directed sequence, so 'principle' is the correct structural classification.

principles.principle: Provide a set of terms designed to represent earth science collection items.
principles.evidence: The ABCD Extension EFG (Extension for Geoscience) is a set of terms designed to represent earth science collection items.

principles.principle: Extend the ABCD schema to integrate geological data, including paleontological and geological collection items.
principles.evidence: Therefore, the Extension for Geosciences (EFG) extends the ABCD schema to integrate geological data, including information about paleontological and geological collection items.

principles.principle: Provide a standard for petrological, mineralogical, and paleontological collection data to facilitate their exchange and publication.
principles.evidence: The aim is to provide a standard for petrological, mineralogical, and paleontological collection data in order to facilitate their exchange and publication.

principles.principle: Publish the extension as an XML Schema Definition (XSD) and manage its ratification through TDWG.
principles.evidence:
- **Download:** [xsd](https://github.com/tdwg/abcd/blob/master/efg/dev/efg.xsd)
- **Status:** Under ratification by TDWG
- **Category:** Technical specification

principles.principle: Support very granular, detailed descriptions of geoscientific objects including observations, specimens, stratigraphy, dates, analyses and integrated host-rock descriptions.
principles.evidence: The EFG schema is very granular and allows a detailed description of geoscientific objects. It comprises a broad range of properties regarding geological and geomorphological observations; geological specimens and their preparations; paleontological, mineral, rock and sediment specimens; anomalous items (e.g. glacial erratics, transported assemblages); stratigraphic and absolute dates; measured stratigraphic sections and borehole logs; identifications (extended to cover rock and mineral classifications, varietal names etc.), analyses (techniques and results e.g. chemical composition of minerals, petrological analysis of rock); integrated description of the host rock as part of a unit record (e.g. mineralisation and alteration of ammonite specimen).

principles.principle: Maintain the schema via a dedicated TDWG Task Group which handles ratification and inquiries during review.
principles.evidence: This Task Group maintains the schema extension, takes care of the ratification process, and is in charge of any inquiries during the current review.

principles.principle: Welcome community involvement from those with interest or experience in geoscientific data standards.
principles.evidence: This Task Group would welcome anyone who has an interest in the standardized description of fossil, mineralogical, and petrological collection objects and / or experience with geoscientific data standards.

principles.principle: The EFG development originated in EU-funded SYNTHESYS and GeoCASe work beginning in 2005 and has been developed by a team of experts from multiple institutions.
principles.evidence: The Development of the ABCDEFG schema for earth science started in 2005. In the framework of the EU-funded project SYNTHESYS the Geosciences Collection Access Service (GeoCASe) portal. The aim is to provide a standard for petrological, mineralogical, and paleontological collection data in order to facilitate their exchange and publication.

principles.principle: Public review and issue-tracking for the draft standard are managed on TDWG's GitHub repositories (EFG repository provided).
principles.evidence: TDWG is now managing the public review of standards on TDWG's GitHub space. Each of these specifications has its own repository: ... EFG - https://github.com/tdwg/efg

standards.notes: No explicit field-level metadata table or ordered workflow was present in the supplied files; the extension itself (XSD) exists at the provided link but its element-level field list was not included in these source excerpts, so only principles/intentions and governance details could be extracted with verbatim evidence.
